rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a holiday would make voting a civic celebration and normalize participation.
rebuttals.objection: That civic-symbolic benefit does not address the binding constraint for low-income workers: they need protected, paid time to vote, not just a more celebratory label for the day.

rebuttals.target: AG1's broader assumption that a national holiday is the right primary mechanism for increasing participation.
rebuttals.objection: A federal Election Day holiday could distract from more targeted reforms, because it is politically easier to pass a calendar change than the access and time-off reforms that actually move turnout, and it may crowd out those better measures.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would directly remove the scheduling barrier to voting.
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give most workers time off: private employers are generally not required to close or provide paid leave. Low-income retail and service workers may still have to work or lose wages to vote, so the holiday would not reliably solve the scheduling barrier and could even widen turnout disparities by helping people with flexible schedules more than constrained workers.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a national holiday is only a symbolic designation and does not itself ensure voting time for private-sector workers.
rebuttals.objection: The objection assumes the holiday would be implemented without accompanying protections. AG1 counters that the federal law creating Election Day as a holiday can and should include job-protected time off to vote for all workers, so the holiday need not be limited to federal employees and can be made a reliable scheduling fix.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national holiday can be made reliable by adding job-protected voting leave.
rebuttals.objection: That answer changes the proposal into a separate voting-time enforcement reform. A holiday by itself does not create universal leave; requiring employer time off is a different policy, so the holiday strategy still is not, on its own, a reliable way to reduce turnout disparities for low-income workers.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that private employers still control workers' schedules even on a national holiday.
rebuttals.objection: AG1 disputes the assumption that a holiday only affects federal employees. It argues that a national holiday changes schools, business hours, community services, transportation schedules, and common workplace practices, so many private-sector workers—especially in retail and service jobs—gain practical time to vote even without special leave legislation.

rebuttals.target: AG1's overall claim that a national Election Day holiday is the best way to increase turnout.
rebuttals.objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself does not meaningfully boost turnout compared with other access reforms. Because the policy would consume attention without reliably improving participation, more targeted measures like state voting-time laws or automatic voter registration are more effective alternatives.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday is a weak standalone turnout reform and should be rejected in favor of other access reforms.
rebuttals.objection: AG1 repeats that the main barrier is scheduling tied to work and school hours, and says a holiday directly expands available time on Election Day by closing schools and altering work and service schedules. It also argues the holiday increases the civic salience of voting, so it can improve turnout even without other reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday will shift the schedules of the workers most constrained by voting-day conflicts.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday does not guarantee that private-sector retail, service, and essential workers will be off or paid to vote. Many will still be scheduled or face unpaid leave, so the groups with the biggest time constraints may remain constrained; the holiday would mainly help people who already have flexible schedules or workplaces that voluntarily close.

rebuttals.target: AG2's objection that the holiday will not reliably change real-world schedules enough to matter.
rebuttals.objection: AG1 reiterates that schools are typically closed, many workplaces adopt holiday hours or shut down, and transportation and community routines change, so the day itself becomes more available for voting. On this view, the holiday directly expands practical voting time for many workers and students and is not merely symbolic.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that holiday-related schedule changes will reliably give the main constrained workers a practical voting window.
rebuttals.objection: Even with schools closed and some holiday-hour adjustments, private employers still decide whether workers are scheduled, and many retail, service, and essential jobs remain open. Therefore the holiday does not reliably create voting time for low-income workers and may leave the people with the strongest scheduling barriers effectively unchanged.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a federal Election Day holiday would remove work-based barriers for many voters, especially low-income workers.
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still have to work and would not reliably gain voting access from the holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday would broadly help low-income workers by making voting easier.
rebuttals.objection: Because the holiday would not reliably remove the main practical barriers for low-income voters, any turnout gains would be limited and uneven, leaving low-income workers disadvantaged relative to better-resourced voters.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a holiday automatically meaningfully increases turnout.
rebuttals.objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's implication that a federal holiday is the best way to improve voting access.
rebuttals.objection: State-level laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more direct and reliable ways to remove voting barriers than a national holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would produce large benefits without much downside.
rebuttals.objection: Because a standalone holiday is likely to yield only limited gains, prioritizing it would consume political attention and resources and could slow or displace more effective reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday would improve access for low-income workers.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday can disrupt school and child-care routines, forcing low-income households to find alternative supervision or rearrange work schedules, which can create extra time and cost burdens that interfere with voting.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday would not disadvantage low-income voters.
rebuttals.objection: Low-income households are less able to absorb disruptions to school and child-care routines, so those holiday-related burdens can fall more heavily on them and make voting harder rather than easier.
